newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway minister sees no glut in European gas market.
newsitem.headline: Norway minister sees no glut in European gas market.

text.p: Norwegian Energy Minister Jens Stoltenberg on Wednesday said he did not foresee any fundamental imbalance in the European gas market, despite a rapid increase in supplies by the end of the decade.
A strong rise in consumption and substitution by gas for other energy sources such as coal should outpace rising supplies, he said.
"The demand for gas in Europe is increasing strongly, so there has to be an increase in the supply," Stoltenberg said in an interview.

"We see a very strong increase in the demand for gas because of a need for more energy and a need for clean energy, such as substituting for coal in different applications. Even with new supplies, I'm sure the balance in the market will not be undermined."

Gas supplies to continental Europe are expected to rise by 25 percent, or 90 billion cubic metres (3.178 trillion cu ft) per year, by 2000, mainly from Norway, Russia, Algeria, the Netherlands and Britain.

Norway will open the taps on the giant Troll field in October, raising total Norwegian supplies to Europe by 36 billion cubic metres (1.271 trillion cu ft) per year to more than 60 billion cubic metres (2.119 trillion cu ft) at peak production early next century.

Stoltenberg said one factor in the growth of gas consumption was its substitution for other energy forms such as coal. A good example of this was a deal clinched early this week with the Czech Republic.

Norway will supply three billion cubic metres (105.9 billion cu ft) per year of gas to the East European country, which will be used mainly to substitute coal as a fuel in households and the medium industry sector. The contract will run from January 1, 1997.
Stoltenberg said a diversity of gas suppliers to Europe was essential for the continued growth of the market.

"There is some kind of common interest between the gas suppliers, in so much as if buyers (distributors) had only one source of supply they would be more reluctant to develop the gas infrastructure and to invest in the huge infrastructure needed to get the gas to their customers," the minister said.
"Because there is more than one source of supply it's easier for the distributors to expand the market which is to the benefit of all suppliers."
Stoltenberg declined to speculate on any liberalisation of the European market, but said deregulation should run across the industry.

"We are interested in a balanced development in the European gas market. The question of deregulation has to be where both the interests of the suppliers and the buyers are taken into consideration. It will not be a good thing if only the supply is liberalised without also doing something at the demand side," Stoltenberg said.
